blocks.text: 1. Leaky ReLU

blocks.alt: A negative input gets a small negative slope while a positive input keeps the same value

blocks.text: ReLU's dying neuron problem, the previous topic's closing weakness, left a genuine, well-documented gap for improvement. Leaky ReLU makes one small, deliberate change specifically to fix this exact issue, while keeping essentially everything else about plain ReLU's behavior intact.
It is the first, simplest of several ReLU variants covered across the rest of this module, each one addressing the exact same underlying weakness in its own particular way.
2. Leaky ReLU's Mathematics

Leaky ReLU takes any real number as input and asks the exact same question plain ReLU asks: is this input positive? If yes, it outputs the input unchanged, exactly like plain ReLU, no difference there at all.

If the input is zero or negative, though, it outputs a small, non-zero fraction of the input instead of exactly zero, the one genuine mathematical difference from plain ReLU, and the entire point of this topic.

blocks.text: 3. The Leak Idea

blocks.alt: ReLU has a hard zero while leaky ReLU lets a small leak through

blocks.text: This connects back to plain ReLU's exactly-zero output for negative inputs, already covered in the previous topic. Leaky ReLU instead outputs a small leak, 0.01 times the input for instance, never exactly zero for a negative input, however small that negative value actually is.

This tiny leak keeps the gradient alive too, a small, non-zero constant instead of plain ReLU's exactly-zero gradient in that same region, the direct mechanism by which this small mathematical change actually solves the dying neuron problem covered earlier in this topic.
4. Fixing the Dying ReLU Problem

blocks.alt: A neuron stuck negative still has a small gradient flow through

blocks.text: This connects directly back to the dying ReLU problem, covered in full depth in the previous topic. A neuron pushed into negative territory under Leaky ReLU still has a tiny, non-zero gradient available, unlike the exactly-zero gradient plain ReLU leaves it with.

This means it can still be nudged back through continued training, rather than staying permanently dead the way a plain ReLU neuron in this same situation genuinely would. This is the direct, complete solution to the specific weakness this entire topic was built to address.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This is a genuinely elegant fix: a single small mathematical change, adding a tiny non-zero slope for negative inputs, directly solves a real, practical training problem without meaningfully changing the function's behavior for positive inputs at all.

blocks.text: 5. The Slope Parameter
The leak's specific size is a chosen parameter, commonly called alpha. A small, fixed value, 0.01 for instance, is the standard, common default choice used in most practical implementations.

This value is deliberately kept small enough that the function still behaves almost exactly like plain ReLU for positive inputs, and only very mildly different for negative ones, preserving most of plain ReLU's original behavior while still providing the genuine fix covered throughout this topic.
6. A Genuine Tradeoff Versus Plain ReLU

blocks.alt: Leaky ReLU fixes dying neurons but adds one extra hyperparameter

blocks.text: A genuine, direct tradeoff exists compared to plain ReLU. Leaky ReLU fixes the dying neuron problem, a real, meaningful improvement already covered throughout this topic. But it also adds one more hyperparameter to choose, the leak size itself.

This is a genuinely small cost, but a real one, covered in further depth in the Hyperparameter Tuning module later in this course, where choosing this kind of additional parameter systematically, rather than guessing, gets covered fully.
7. What Real, Practical Experience Shows
Real, practical experience shows Leaky ReLU sometimes genuinely outperforms plain ReLU, especially on networks that show clear, observable signs of dead neurons during training.

It also sometimes performs about the same as plain ReLU in practice, meaning the improvement is genuinely real but not always dramatic, a nuanced, honest picture worth keeping in mind rather than assuming Leaky ReLU is always a strict, guaranteed upgrade over plain ReLU.
8. The Computational Cost

blocks.alt: Leaky ReLU is nearly as fast as ReLU

blocks.text: This connects back to the computational simplicity already covered in the ReLU topic. Leaky ReLU costs only slightly more to compute than plain ReLU, given the one small additional multiplication needed for negative inputs.

It remains considerably cheaper than sigmoid or tanh's exponential calculations, meaning this genuine fix comes at essentially no meaningful computational cost compared to the far more expensive alternatives already covered earlier in this module.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When Leaky ReLU Is Worth Trying

blocks.alt: Many dead neurons observed points toward trying leaky ReLU

blocks.text: A network using plain ReLU that shows clear signs of dead, permanently inactive neurons, exactly the problem covered throughout the previous topic, is a genuinely direct, well-motivated case worth trying Leaky ReLU first.

A brand new network, with no observed dying-neuron problem yet, can genuinely still start with plain ReLU as a reasonable, simpler starting point, only switching to Leaky ReLU if that specific, real problem actually shows up during training.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Leaky ReLU makes one small, deliberate change to fix ReLU's dying neuron problem.
It behaves exactly like ReLU for positive inputs, but outputs a small, non-zero fraction of negative inputs.
This tiny leak keeps the gradient alive too, never exactly zero the way plain ReLU's gradient is for negative inputs.
A neuron in negative territory can still be nudged back through training, rather than staying permanently dead.
The leak's size, commonly called alpha, is typically a small fixed value like 0.01.
It fixes the dying neuron problem at the cost of one additional hyperparameter to choose.
Real experience shows a genuine but not always dramatic improvement over plain ReLU.
It costs only slightly more to compute than plain ReLU, still far cheaper than sigmoid or tanh.
Next up: PReLU, which makes this same leak size itself a value the network actually learns during training.
